name: Independent identically distributed
type_shape: An iid sample of p-dimensional vectors whose distribution can change with the dimension and sample size. Dependence among coordinates within a vector is allowed.
semantic_boundary: An iid sample of p-dimensional vectors whose distribution can change with the dimension and sample size. Dependence among coordinates within a vector is allowed.

members.statement_original: To be precise, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ denote independent identically distributed $p$-dimensional random vectors with distribution function $F$. Note that formally $F$ depends on the dimension $p$, which varies with $n$, but we will not reflect this dependence in our notation throughout this paper.

name: Symmetric kernel
type_shape: Measurable symmetric vector kernel of positive integer order m and its finite expectation. Kernel dimension d need not equal observation dimension p.
semantic_boundary: Measurable symmetric vector kernel of positive integer order m and its finite expectation. Kernel dimension d need not equal observation dimension p.

members.local_label: Section 2 — kernel and expectation parameter, equations (2.1)-(2.2)
members.source_heading: Section 2 — kernel and expectation parameter, equations (2.1)-(2.2)
members.statement_original:
For some positive integer $m$ let
\[
h=(h_1,\ldots,h_d)^\top:(\mathbb R^p)^m\to\mathbb R^d\tag{2.1}
\]
denote a measurable symmetric function with finite expectation
\[
\theta_F=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)^\top=\mathbb E_F[h(X_1,\ldots,X_m)]\in\mathbb R^d,\tag{2.2}
\]
which defines our parameter of interest.

naming_context.text: where $h_i$, the ith component of the vector $h$ in (2.1), is a symmetric kernel of order $m$.

name: U-statistic
type_shape: Complete order-m U-statistic with each increasing tuple counted once. Coordinate U_i is repeated explicitly in (2.6). No particular pairwise dependence measure or covariance kernel is assumed.
semantic_boundary: Complete order-m U-statistic with each increasing tuple counted once. Coordinate U_i is repeated explicitly in (2.6). No particular pairwise dependence measure or covariance kernel is assumed.

members.statement_original:
In order to estimate the parameter $\theta_F$ we consider the U-statistic of order $m$
\[
U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)^\top=\binom nm^{-1}\sum_{1\leq l_1<\ldots<l_m\leq n}h(X_{l_1},\ldots,X_{l_m}).\tag{2.3}
\]

name: Dependence measure
type_shape: Pairwise kernel-expectation dependence measures arranged in an upper-triangle vector. The source uses vech for columns above the diagonal, excluding the diagonal; this convention is not replaced by the usual lower-triangle convention.
semantic_boundary: Pairwise kernel-expectation dependence measures arranged in an upper-triangle vector. The source uses vech for columns above the diagonal, excluding the diagonal; this convention is not replaced by the usual lower-triangle convention.

members.local_label: Example 2.1 — pairwise dependence and upper-triangle vectorization, equation (2.4)
members.source_heading: Example 2.1 — pairwise dependence and upper-triangle vectorization, equation (2.4)
members.statement_original:
To be precise, for $1\leq i<j\leq p$ let
\[
d_{ij}=d(X_{1i},X_{1j})=\mathbb E_F[\widetilde h(X_{1i},X_{1j},\ldots,X_{mi},X_{mj})]\tag{2.4}
\]
denote a dependence measure between the ith and jth components of the random vector $X_1=(X_{11},\ldots,X_{1p})^\top$, which can be expressed as the expectation of a kernel $\widetilde h:\mathbb R^{2m}\to\mathbb R$ of order $m$ evaluated at $(X_{1i},X_{1j},\ldots,X_{mi},X_{mj})$. In this case the function $h$ in (2.1) is defined by
\[
h(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=\operatorname{vech}\big((h_{ij}(X_1,\ldots,X_m))_{i,j=1,\ldots,p}\big)
=\operatorname{vech}\big((\widetilde h(X_{1i},X_{1j},\ldots,X_{mi},X_{mj}))_{i,j=1,\ldots,p}\big),
\]
where the second equality defines the functions $h_{ij}:\mathbb R^{pm}\to\mathbb R$ in an obvious manner and $\operatorname{vech}(\cdot)$ is the operator that stacks the columns above the diagonal of a symmetric $p\times p$ matrix as a vector with $d=p(p-1)/2$ components. Note that the index $(i,j)$ in the definition of the function $h_{ij}$ is only used to emphasize that each $h_{ij}$ acts on different components of the vectors $X_1,\ldots,X_m$. Similarly, the vector $\theta_F$ is defined by $\theta_F=\operatorname{vech}\big((d_{ij})_{i,j=1,\ldots,p}\big)$,

name: Relevant hypotheses
type_shape: Composite null that all coordinate magnitudes are at most a positive threshold, versus any exceedance. The threshold is not zero and the alternative inequality is strict.
semantic_boundary: Composite null that all coordinate magnitudes are at most a positive threshold, versus any exceedance. The threshold is not zero and the alternative inequality is strict.

members.statement_original:
Recall that, in this paper, we are not interested in testing the “classical” hypotheses $H_0:\theta_F=0$ versus $H_1:\theta_F\neq0$, but want to investigate if at least one of the components $\theta_i$ of the vector $\theta_F=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)^\top$ exceeds a given threshold $\Delta>0$, that is
\[
H_0:\max_{i=1}^d|\theta_i|\leq\Delta\quad\text{versus}\quad H_1:\max_{i=1}^d|\theta_i|>\Delta,\tag{2.5}
\]
where $\Delta$ denotes the largest deviation that is still considered as negligible. Hypotheses of this form are often called relevant hypotheses.

name: Non-degenerate
type_shape: Uncentered first conditional projection and its variance, with the source non-degeneracy criterion. This records the definition without imposing positivity on every coordinate.
semantic_boundary: Uncentered first conditional projection and its variance, with the source non-degeneracy criterion. This records the definition without imposing positivity on every coordinate.

\zeta_{1,i}=\operatorname{Var}_F(h_{1,i}(X_1))\quad\text{and}\quad
h_{1,i}(x)=\mathbb E_F[h_i(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\mid X_1=x].\tag{2.8}
\]
If $\zeta_{1,i}>0$, the kernel $h_i$ of the statistic $U_i$ is called non-degenerate. Note that this property depends on the kernel $h_i$ and on the distribution $F$.

name: Orlicz norm
type_shape: The source exponential Orlicz quantity for scalar variables. The parameter range beta in (0,2] comes from the assumptions; for beta<1 it is conventionally a quasi-norm rather than a norm, but the source wording is preserved.
semantic_boundary: The source exponential Orlicz quantity for scalar variables. The parameter range beta in (0,2] comes from the assumptions; for beta<1 it is conventionally a quasi-norm rather than a norm, but the source wording is preserved.

members.statement_original:
In what follows, we will need the function $\psi_\beta(x)=\exp(x^\beta)-1$ and the corresponding Orlicz norm
\[
\|Z\|_{\psi_\beta}:=\inf\{\nu>0:\mathbb E[\psi_\beta(|Z|/\nu)]\leq1\}\tag{2.13}
\]
of a real-valued random variable $Z$.

name: Uniform tail probability decay
type_shape: All three source conditions: exponential centered-kernel tail, bounded projection variance and projection fourth moment. B_n is only required to be nonnegative; it is not silently assumed uniformly positive or bounded.
semantic_boundary: All three source conditions: exponential centered-kernel tail, bounded projection variance and projection fourth moment. B_n is only required to be nonnegative; it is not silently assumed uniformly positive or bounded.

members.statement_original:
For some constant $\beta\in(0,2]$ there exist a non-negative sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ and a constant $D>0$ such that for all $d=d(n)$, $n\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\|h_i(X_1,\ldots,X_m)-\theta_i\|_{\psi_\beta}\leq B_n,\qquad
\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\zeta_{1,i}\leq D,\qquad
\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\mathbb E_F[(h_{1,i}(X_1)-\theta_i)^4]\leq DB_n^2.
\]

naming_context.text: Assumption (A1) is a technical condition that captures a uniform tail probability decay from which we will deduce concentration inequalities for the components of the U-statistic defined in (2.3).

name: Uniform non-degeneracy requirement
type_shape: Uniform positive projection variance only for parameters bounded away from zero. The strict cutoff and strict lower bound, and the empty-minimum value, are preserved.
semantic_boundary: Uniform positive projection variance only for parameters bounded away from zero. The strict cutoff and strict lower bound, and the empty-minimum value, are preserved.

members.statement_original: There exist constants $\underline b>0$ and $c\in(0,\Delta)$ such that $\min_{1\leq i\leq d,|\theta_i|>c}\zeta_{1,i}>\underline b$ for all $d=d(n)$, $n\in\mathbb N$. Here and in the following, a minimum over the empty set is defined as $+\infty$.

naming_context.text: Assumption (A2) is a uniform non-degeneracy requirement which is a standard condition for deriving Gaussian approximation results,

name: Correlation
type_shape: Off-diagonal correlation summability condition for the Gumbel approximation, with each stated correlation strictly between minus one and one. It is not needed by the bootstrap theorems.
semantic_boundary: Off-diagonal correlation summability condition for the Gumbel approximation, with each stated correlation strictly between minus one and one. It is not needed by the bootstrap theorems.

members.statement_original:
Let $\kappa_{i,j}=\operatorname{Corr}_F(h_{1,i}(X_1),h_{1,j}(X_1))\in(-1,1)$ denote the correlation between $h_{1,i}(X_1)$ and $h_{1,j}(X_1)$. There exist a constant $\epsilon>0$ and a sequence $\gamma_n=o(1)$ such that for all $d=d(n)$, $n\in\mathbb N$
\[
\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq d}\frac{|\kappa_{i,j}|}{\sqrt{1-\kappa_{i,j}^2}}
\exp\left(-\frac{(2-\epsilon)\log d}{1+|\kappa_{i,j}|}\right)\leq\gamma_n.
\]

type_shape: Composite null class for the Gumbel-calibrated test. The source opening says distributions on R^d although the sampling class F was defined on R^p; both source conventions are preserved.

members.local_label: Section 2.1 — composite null distribution class, equations (2.14)-(2.15)
members.source_heading: Section 2.1 — composite null distribution class, equations (2.14)-(2.15)
members.statement_original:
For a precise statement consider the set of all distribution functions on $\mathbb R^d$ satisfying Assumptions (A1) - (A3), and define
\[
V_0:=\{z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^\top\in\mathbb R^d\mid\max_{1\leq i\leq d}|z_i|\leq\Delta\}\tag{2.14}
\]
as the parameter space corresponding to the null hypothesis in (2.5). Note that these sets depend on $n$ (through the dimension $d=d(n)$). We define
\[
\mathcal H_0(\Delta):=\{F\in\mathcal F\mid\theta_F\in V_0,\ F\text{ satisfies Assumptions (A1), (A2), (A3)}\}\tag{2.15}
\]
as the set of distribution functions satisfying the null hypothesis (and the basic assumptions) with existing expectation $\mathbb E_F[U]$. Note that $\mathcal H_0(\Delta)$ depends on the constants $\underline b$, $D$ and on $n$ (through the dimension $d=d(n)$ and sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$) which is not reflected in our notation.

name: Alternatives
type_shape: Uniform alternative class with maximum parameter magnitude at least Delta plus the specified separation. The lower bound is weak and only Assumption (A1) enters the class. The bootstrap theorem substitutes a logarithmically inflated argument.
semantic_boundary: Uniform alternative class with maximum parameter magnitude at least Delta plus the specified separation. The lower bound is weak and only Assumption (A1) enters the class. The bootstrap theorem substitutes a logarithmically inflated argument.

members.statement_original:
Next we turn to the consistency of the test (2.11) and define
\[
V(c)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d\mid\max_{1\leq i\leq d}|z_i|\geq\Delta+cB_n((\log d)/n)^{1/2}\}
\]
as a set of alternatives (note that for a bounded kernel $h$ the sequence $B_n$ can be chosen as a constant sequence). We will study the power of the test (2.11) against alternatives in the set
\[
\mathcal H_1(c)=\{F\in\mathcal F\mid\theta_F\in V(c);\ F\text{ satisfies Assumption (A1)}\}.\tag{2.18}
\]

name: Bootstrap analogue
type_shape: Empirical bootstrap U-statistic, conditionally iid resampling the observed vectors with replacement. Repeated original observations can enter a tuple despite its distinct bootstrap indices.
semantic_boundary: Empirical bootstrap U-statistic, conditionally iid resampling the observed vectors with replacement. Repeated original observations can enter a tuple despite its distinct bootstrap indices.

members.statement_original:
To be precise, let $X_1^*,\ldots,X_n^*$ be drawn with replacement from $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ and define for $i=1,\ldots,d$ by
\[
U_i^*=\binom nm^{-1}\sum_{1\leq l_1<\ldots<l_m\leq n}h_i(X_{l_1}^*,\ldots,X_{l_m}^*)\tag{2.19}
\]
a bootstrap analogue of the statistic introduced in (2.6).

name: V-statistic
type_shape: Full V-statistic including repeated indices, equal to the conditional expectation of U_i*. This is not the original distinct-index U-statistic.
semantic_boundary: Full V-statistic including repeated indices, equal to the conditional expectation of U_i*. This is not the original distinct-index U-statistic.

members.statement_original:
Note that the conditional expectation of $U_i^*$ given $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is given by the V-statistic
\[
V_i=\mathbb E_F[U_i^*\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n]=\frac1{n^m}\sum_{l_1,\ldots,l_m=1}^n h_i(X_{l_1},\ldots,X_{l_m}).\tag{2.20}
\]

name: Truncated version

members.statement_original:
We finally define
\[
\mathcal T_n^*=\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\frac{(U_i^*-V_i+V_{i,\Delta})^2-V_{i,\Delta}^2}{2\widehat\sigma_i\Delta}\tag{2.22}
\]

\]
